newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. conditionally OKs Bell Atlantic, Nynex merger.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. conditionally OKs Bell Atlantic, Nynex merger.

text.p: New York state utility regulators Thursday approved the $23 billion Nynex Corp. and Bell Atlantic Corp. merger, subject to conditions the regional telephone giants must agree to within 10 days.
Consumer groups opposed to the merger that have demanded rate rebates for New York customers blasted the state Public Service Commission's decision as a sellout.

New York became the last state in Nynex's six-state service region to approve the merger, which still faces hurdles in Washington. The deal has come under increased scrutiny recently from the Justice Department and the Federal Trade Commission.

Public Service Commission Chairman John O'Mara said in an interview that, while there would be no immediate rate reduction as a result, "We have attached conditions that we believe will bring rate reduction."
The companies welcomed the decision but said in a joint statement that they were still assessing the conditions.

The merger of the Baby Bells -- which will create a phone company serving 12 states and Washington that will be the nation's biggest local phone operator -- still faces potential hurdles in Washington and New York.
All three commission members voted for the merger and the conditions in a 15-minute meeting in Albany, the state capital.
The conditions include a requirement the merged company hire up to 1,000 new support staff by the end of 1997 to shore up customer service for New York state local phone customers.
The commission also said the combined company must not relocate major business functions in New York state before the merger.
The panel required the new corporate headquarters be in New York, which New York-based Nynex and Philadelphia-based Bell Atlantic have already said they would do.

The regulators focused on improving customer service for local phone customers in New York, where consumer groups have berated Nynex for offering what they say is the lowest quality customer service in the nation.

The plan calls on Nynex to accelerate capital spending to improve customer service. Previously, Nynex's New York Telephone local service unit was ordered to boost such spending by $1 billion over five years.
New York Telephone already operates under a plan adopted by regulators in September 1995 that provides a set of carrot-and-stick incentives for it to improve service.
The conditional merger plan would require at least $500 million of the $1 billion to be spent within the next two years.
Consumer groups were swift to criticise the commission's decision.

"We are outraged that this commission approved a merger that is completely anticompetitive," said Robert Ceisler, of the N.Y. Citizens Utility Board, a ratepayers' group. "The commission has sanctioned a more powerful and richer monopoly."

Consumer advocates had demanded the commission at a minimum force Nynex to give consumers immediate rate rebates to compensate for the reduced competition and greater efficiencies expected to result from the merger.

"The commission has utterly failed to improve conditions for New York ratepayers," Ceisler said. "We believe New York would have been better off if Bell Atlantic had come into the state and competed with Nynex."
Ceisler said the merger will delay the arrival of lower rates for New York consumers promised by state and federal deregulation efforts in recent years.

Other conditions for approval include having Bell Atlantic pledge to observe existing agreements between regulators and Nynex, that Nynex employee pension funds be protected, and that Bell Atlantic grant regulators access to its records.

The deal also faces review by New York State Attorney General Dennis Vacco, who has said the merger would strengthen Nynex's existing monopoly and was a bad deal for residential and small business customers.
Nynex stock rose 25 cents to $47.625 while Bell Atlantic fell 12.5 cents to $63.25, both in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
